title: Emergency Radio Basics
summary: How to operate hand-held radios, select frequencies, and use protocols during emergency scenarios.

sections.heading: Step 1 — Understand Radio Frequencies
sections.body: Select the correct band: FRS/GMRS (462 MHz) are common for short-range walkie-talkies. VHF (136-174 MHz) works best in open terrain and marine environments (Channel 16 is the international distress channel). UHF (400-470 MHz) is better inside buildings and wooded areas. HAM bands offer long-distance communication.
sections.warning: Do not transmit on emergency, police, or military frequencies unless in a life-or-death emergency.
sections.image_description: A spectrum diagram showing FRS, VHF, and UHF bands with ranges

sections.heading: Step 2 — Conserve Battery Power
sections.body: Radios consume significant energy, especially during transmission. To prolong battery life: 1. Turn down display backlighting and volume. 2. Set power output to 'Low' (1W or 0.5W) for close-range team communications. 3. Establish pre-arranged schedules to check-in (e.g., 5 minutes at the top of every hour) and turn off the radio in between.
sections.warning: Always keep a spare set of lithium batteries or a hand-crank solar charger in your emergency kit.
sections.image_description: Hand-crank radio charger with a battery level indicator

sections.heading: Step 3 — Apply Transmission Protocols
sections.body: Keep transmissions concise. Listen for 5 seconds before speaking to ensure the channel is clear. Speak clearly in a normal voice, 2-3 inches from the microphone. Use standard brevity codes: say 'Over' when finished speaking; 'Out' when ending the conversation; and 'Say Again' to request repeat. Use phonetic alphabet (Alpha, Bravo, Charlie) to spell out names or coordinates.
sections.warning: Never use the distress call 'MAYDAY' unless life, vessel, or property is in immediate, grave danger.
sections.image_description: Person speaking calmly into a hand-held radio

sections.heading: Step 4 — Optimize Antenna and Location
sections.body: Radio waves travel line-of-sight. For maximum range: 1. Climb to the highest accessible ground (hilltops, roofs). 2. Keep the antenna pointing vertically. 3. Avoid transmitting close to concrete walls, metal structures, or power lines. 4. If using HF, construct a simple dipol wire antenna hung between two trees.
sections.warning: Never touch or hold the antenna during transmission as this degrades signal and can cause RF burns.
sections.image_description: Person standing on a hilltop holding a radio antenna vertically

when_to_use: When standard cellular networks, internet connections, and telephone lines are offline during a regional disaster.
do_not: Transmit on emergency frequencies without a true emergency
Leave the radio scanning or transmitting continuously
Use complex language (keep messages short, plain, and clear)
